notes.b: Marriage is both a social institution, recognised by society, and a legal status, recognised and protected by the State. It is a voluntary commitment that is intended to be lasting.
points: A marriage is a union of two people who freely agree to it, entered into through a civil or religious ceremony that is legally recognised. Because both must agree freely, nobody can be forced into it.
Marriage is a union to the exclusion of all others, so a person may be married to only one person at a time. Marrying again while the first marriage is still valid is bigamy, which is a crime.
Living together as a couple and remaining faithful to each other are part of what marriage involves, and a full definition includes both.

Marriage creates legal rights and duties between the spouses (husband and wife), including inheritance rights and a duty of financial support for the spouse and children. This is why it is a legal status as well as a personal commitment.
notes.tip: If asked to define marriage, give: legally recognised, two people, to the exclusion of all others, plus living together or faithfulness. Do not define it as a union between a man and a woman, because same-sex couples may now marry.

notes.b: The State gives marriage special protection in the Constitution, and the law has changed over time about who can marry and how couples are recognised.
points: Article 41 of the Constitution (Article 41.3 deals with marriage) pledges the State to guard the institution of marriage, on which the family is founded, with special care, and to protect it against attack.
After the marriage equality referendum on 22 May 2015, the Constitution says marriage may be contracted in accordance with law by two persons without distinction as to their sex.
The Marriage Act 2015 gave this effect, in force from 16 November 2015, so same-sex couples marry on the same legal terms as opposite-sex couples.

Civil partnership, created by the Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010, gave same-sex couples rights and duties similar to marriage. It is a different legal status, not marriage.
Civil partnership is no longer available to new couples, but existing civil partnerships remain valid. Civil partners who marry each other end their civil partnership.

A marriage can be a civil ceremony (conducted by a registrar or a civil solemniser) or a religious ceremony (by a priest, minister or other person registered as a solemniser). A secular or humanist ceremony is possible with a registered solemniser. Each has the same legal effect once registered.
notes.tip: Civil partnership is not the same as marriage, so say it is similar in rights but a separate status. Do not say partners must be of opposite sex, because the Marriage Act 2015 removed that.

notes.h: Legal requirements for a valid marriage in Ireland
notes.b: The law sets conditions so that a marriage is entered into freely, by people who are able to marry, and is properly recorded. A marriage that fails these conditions may be void or voidable, and a court can declare it invalid through legal nullity.
points: Age: both people must be at least 18. There is no exception for 16- and 17-year-olds, because the minimum age is 18 for everyone.
Free to marry: neither person may already be married or in a civil partnership, because a person can be married to only one person at a time.

Consent: both must consent freely, and consent obtained by force, threat or pressure is not valid. Both must also understand what they are doing, so a person who cannot understand the nature of marriage cannot validly marry (this is called capacity).
Prohibited degrees: the couple may not be too closely related, by blood or, in some cases, by marriage or adoption.

Notice: both must give notice of their intention to marry, in person, to a civil registration service (the registrar of the area) at least three months before the wedding. This applies to civil, religious and secular ceremonies.
They bring the documents the registrar requires with the notice, for example identification and a declaration that there is no impediment (nothing in law to stop the marriage).

Formalities: the ceremony is conducted by an authorised person, a registrar or a registered solemniser. The venue is one the registrar has approved (for a civil ceremony), inspected in advance, or a place suitable for the religion. Two witnesses must be present and the required declarations made.
Place: the wedding must take place in a registered building, such as a register office or registered church, or in an approved venue inspected in advance by a registrar.

Registration: the couple and the two witnesses sign the register at the ceremony, and the marriage is then registered. A marriage certificate can be obtained afterwards. The Civil Registration Act 2004 (as amended) governs notice, solemnisers and registration.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for four conditions with a reason. The usual four are age 18, voluntary consent, free to marry (not already married) and three months' notice to the registrar. Give four distinct conditions and do not repeat one in different words. Remember the couple sign the register as well as the witnesses.

notes.b: A marriage that breaks the legal requirements is not always treated the same way. The law separates marriages that were never valid from those that are valid until a court ends them.
points: A void marriage was never valid in law, for example because one person was already married or in a civil partnership, they were within the prohibited degrees, one was under 18, or the formalities were not followed. A court decree is still sought to settle the status.
A voidable marriage is valid until a court annuls it, for example because one spouse did not freely consent, or because one spouse is unable to sustain a normal marital relationship.
A marriage that cannot be consummated (no sexual relations after the ceremony because of an inability to do so) can be annulled.
Only the Circuit Court or High Court can grant a nullity decree, and an agreement between the couple cannot annul a marriage. The court process is called legal nullity.
notes.tip: If you mention consummation, say inability to consummate, not failure to consummate, because the legal ground is inability to sustain a normal marital relationship.

keyTerms.definition: A voluntary, legally recognised union of two people that excludes all others and carries legal rights and duties for both spouses.
The practice of having only one spouse at a time.
The official who receives the notice of intention to marry, approves venues and registers marriages.
Close family relationships, by blood or by marriage, within which two people may not marry each other.
Sexual intercourse between the spouses after the marriage ceremony.
A marriage that was never valid in law, for example because one partner was already married.
A marriage that remains valid until a court annuls it, for example because of inability to consummate the marriage.
A legal status for two people of the same sex that gives them rights similar to marriage but is not marriage.

factCards.term: Four legal conditions for a valid marriage in Ireland
factCards.definition: Both partners are at least 18; both are free to marry; both consent voluntarily; three months' written notice has been given to the registrar of the area.

factCards.term: Witnesses at an Irish civil marriage
factCards.definition: Two witnesses must be present and sign the register after the ceremony.

factCards.term: Notice period before a wedding in Ireland
factCards.definition: Three months' written notice of intention to marry must be given to the registrar of the area.
Article 41.3 commits the State to guard the institution of marriage with special care.

factCards.term: Legislation allowing same-sex marriage in Ireland
factCards.definition: The Marriage Act 2015, which followed the 2015 referendum on marriage equality.

factCards.term: Legislation creating civil partnership in Ireland
factCards.definition: The Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010.

questions.prompt: Name two conditions that must be met for a marriage to be legally valid in Ireland, and explain each briefly.
questions.model: Any two of the following, each explained: both partners must be at least 18 years of age; both must be free to marry, meaning neither is already married or in a civil partnership; both must consent voluntarily; written notice of intention to marry must be given to the registrar of the area at least three months before the wedding; the ceremony must take place in a registered building or an approved venue; two witnesses must be present and sign the register after the ceremony.

questions.prompt: Outline the steps a couple must follow to have a legally valid civil marriage in Ireland, from giving notice to registration of the marriage, and explain why each step matters.
questions.model: Notice: written notice of intention to marry is given to the registrar of the area at least three months before the wedding, so the registrar can check that the couple are free to marry. Venue: the ceremony takes place in a registered building or an approved venue, or at a location temporarily registered by licence, so that the marriage is recognised by the State. Eligibility: both partners must be at least 18, free to marry and not within the prohibited degrees of relationship. Consent: both partners must consent voluntarily, which protects each from being forced into marriage. Ceremony: two witnesses must be present. Registration: the couple and the two witnesses sign the civil register immediately after the ceremony, creating the official record that makes the marriage legally recognised.
